¶
'''body-guard''' (bod′i-gärd), ''n.'' One who protects or defends the person; a life-guard; collectively, the guard charged with the protection of some person, as a prince or an officer; hence, retinue; attendance; following.
{{smaller block|It might possibly be convenient that, when the Parliament assembled, the King should repair to Westminster with a ''body-guard''.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., ix.}}}}

'''body-hoop''' (bod′i-höp), ''n.'' A band securing the arris pieces of a built mast.

'''body-horse''' (bod′i-hôrs), ''n.'' A shaft-horse. [Prov. Eng.]

'''body-loop''' (bod′i-löp), ''n.'' A strap or iron arm connecting a wagon-body with the gearing.

'''body-louse''' (bod′i-lous), ''n.'' A kind of louse, the ''Pediculus corporis'' or ''P. vestimenti'', which is parasitic on man. {{smaller|It is generally found on the body, or concealed in the clothing, while the ''Pediculus capitis'', or head-louse, infests the head.}}

'''body-servant''' (bod′i-sėr″vạnt), ''n.'' A servant who waits upon or accompanies his employer; a valet; a personal attendant.

'''body-snatcher''' (bod′i-snach″ėr), ''n.'' One who secretly disinters the bodies of the dead as subjects for dissection, or for the purpose of exacting a ransom; a resurrectionist.

'''body-snatching''' (bod′i-snach″ing), ''n.'' The act of robbing a grave to obtain a subject for dissection.

'''body-varnish''' (bod′i-vär″nish), ''n.'' A thick and quick-drying copal varnish, used for carriages and other objects that are to be polished.

'''body-wall''' (bod′i-wâl), ''n.'' In ''zoöl.'', the general envelop or parietes of a body, especially of a low organism; a cell-wall.

'''body-whorl''' (bod′i-hwėrl), ''n.'' The last-formed and generally largest whorl of a univalve shell. See ''univalve''.

'''Boëdromia''' (bō-ẹ̄-drō′mi-ä̤), ''n. pl.'' See ''Boëdromion''.

'''bog-butter''' (bog′but″ėr), ''n.'' A fatty spermaceti-like mineral resin, composed of carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen, found in masses in peat-bogs.

''Böhme'', a Bohemian, ''Böhmen'', Bohemia.]   A genus of dicotyledonous plants, natural order ''Urticaceæ'', allied to the nettle, but without its stinging hairs. {{smaller|A number}} of species yield tenacious fibers, used for making ropes, twine, net, and sewing-thread. The most important species is ''B. nivea'', a shrubby plant of China and the East Indies, which affords the valuable rhea-fiber or grass-cloth

Puya'', from which the Puya-fiber is obtained, is now referred to the genus ''Maoutia''. See ''grass-cloth''.

'''boggify†''', ''v. t.''   [< ''bog''<sup>1</sup> + ''-i-fy.'']   To make boggy.

'''bogging†''' (bog′ing), ''n.''   [Early mod. E., perhaps a var. of *''bagging'' for ''badging'', verbal n. of ''badge''<sup>2</sup>; cf. ''bodger''<sup>2</sup>.]   Peddling; hawking.   ''N. E. D.''

'''boggish<sup>1</sup>''' (bog′ish), ''a.''   [< ''bog''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Boggy.

'''boggish<sup>2</sup>†''', ''a.''   [ME., written ''boggisshe, boggysche''; < ''bog''<sup>3</sup> (not found in ME.) + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Bold; puffed up; boastful.

'''boggle<sup>1</sup>''', ''n.'' A dialectal form of ''bogle''.

'''boggle<sup>2</sup>''' (bog′l), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''boggled'', ppr. ''boggling''.   [Early mod. E. also ''bogle, buggel'', < ''boggle''<sup>1</sup> = ''bogle'', a specter, with ref. to the shying of a horse at unusual objects; cf. ME. ''bogelen'', occurring but once, in the sense of ‘deny,’ i. e., scare off.]   '''1.''' To take alarm; start with fright; shy, as a horse.
{{smaller block|When a sinner is first tempted to the commission of a more gross and notorious sin, his conscience is apt to ''boggle'' and start at it, he doth it with great difficulty and regret.
{{right|''Tillotson'', Works, I. x.}}}}
{{smaller block|We start and ''boggle'' at every unusual appearance.
{{right|''Granville.''}}}}

'''2.''' To hesitate; stop, as if afraid to proceed, or as if impeded by unforeseen difficulties; waver;<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
